into two parts. Why, however, was the tremor for many days? For Campania did not cease to tremble continuously, more gently indeed, but with immense damage, as it shook what was pressed and shattered. For those things which were distressing it for falling, it was not to be pushed, but to be agitated. Clearly, not all the spirit had exited yet, but with the greater part of itself emitted, it still wandered. Among the arguments by which it is proven that these things are done by spirit, there is no reason why you should doubt to place this also: when the greatest tremor is issued, by which cities and lands have been ravaged, nor can another follow it afterwards, but after the greatest force, the tremors are light, which it made more vehemently when the winds were struggling for an exit. Then the remains of the residual spirit cannot do the same, nor is there need for a fight for them, since they have already found a way, and they follow that by which the first and greatest force escaped. I also judge this worthy of memory to be known by a most learned and serious man: for by chance, when it happened, he was bathing. He affirmed that he saw in the bath the Thessalian tiles, with which the floor was paved, being separated one from the other, and thus being joined and separated; and the water was sometimes received into the fissures as the pavement receded, sometimes boiled and was expelled when it was compressed. I heard the same man telling that he saw soft materials tremble more softly and more frequently than the hard nature. Nor is it, O Lucilius, a man excellent regarding the causes themselves. These things now which pertain to the strengthening of minds, which it is more important to become stronger by nature than more learned. If one is not made without the other. For strength does not come to the mind from elsewhere than from good arts, than from the contemplation of nature. For what has this very calamity not strengthened and raised up against everyone? For why should I fear a man or even a beast? Why should I fear a dart or a spear?

Nam quattuor negocio est dicimus attributa continentia cum ipso negocio et in gestone negocio adiuncta negocio: quae gestu negotio consequuntur. Itaque incontinentibus cum ipso negocio: et in gestione negotii signum est. In his quae gestum negotium consequunt iudicatum est. In his autem quae adiuncta sunt negocio coparabile est. In attributis uero personae credibile est. Ita uidemus et locus argumentorum et res et exitus certis rationibus sibi esse copulata. Nulla itaque uideatur esse confusio quod probabile argumentum iadudum in tria diuisi mus nunc in quattuor: quia id quod fere solet fieri duo in se continet: signum et credibile.

Quod in opinione positum est unum habet in se: id est iudicatum quod het ad haec quanda similitudinem similiter in se unum continet: id est comparabile. Itaque probabile argumentum in quattuor partes nunc diuiditur. Nam aut signum est aut credibile: aut iudicatum: aut comparabile. Signum est quod sub sensum aliquem cadit et quiddam significat quod ex ipso profectu uidetur: quod aut ante fuerit: aut in ipso negocio: aut post fit secutum: et tamen indiget testimonii et grauis confirmationis: ut cruor: fuga: pallor: puluis: et quae his sunt similia. Credibile est: quod sine ullo teste auditoris opinione confirmatur hoc modo. Nemo est qui non liberos suos incolumes et beatos esse cupiat. Iudicatum est res assensione: aut auctoritate: aut iudicio alicuius: aut aliquorum coprobata. Id tribus in generibus spectatur: religioso: communi: et approbato. Religiosum est quod iurati legis bus iudicauerunt. Comune est quod omnes comuniter parant et secuti sunt: huiusmodi est: ut maioribus natu assurgatur: ut supplicatium misereatur.

Eta est. Nam tumultus auditus est. Hic tumultus signum est: sed signum quod sub auriu sensum cadit. Ita et reliqua similia. Veru hoc argumenti genus iugnum non satis ad fide ualet: sed alterius fit maioris argumenti indiget approbatione. Ita probabile quidem est argumentum: sed non ualidum semper quae hoc argumento coniectura tractat. Et ideo aut aliud firmius argumentum. aut testimonium requirit. Sed quod paulo ante dixi fignum esse in eo quod fere solet fieri. Vriq cum dico ex itinere uenit. nam multus in calceis puluis est. et hominem occidit. nam cruentus est. Argumentu facio ex his quae fere solent fieri. nam qui ex itinere uenit solet fieri ut puluerulentus sit. et qui homine occidit solet fieri ut cruentus sit. Ex signo uero in oia tempora circa factum facere possumus argumentum: utputa: occidisti hominem: quia cruentus es. et hic cruor fignum est. Occidisti autem hoiem: tempus praeteritum. Deinde occidis hominem. nam uulnus infigis: fignum est. Occidis homine: tps praesens. Deinde occidere uis homine. nam armatus incedis: hic armatus incedis: fignum est. Oc cidere uis homine: tempus futurum. Ita fignum ad omne tempus argumentum est. Credibile est quod sine ullo teste auditoris opinione firmatur hoc mo. Credibile est inquit argumentu: quod per seipsum fidem facit. Neq ad probandu desiderat teste. Sed facile cum prolatum fuerit apud opinionem et sententiam iudicis persuadetur. Hoc credibile in eo esse diximus quod fere solet fieri: et rursus in attributis personae. Ita in exemplo quod subdidit Cicero utrumque et uideamus. Nemo est inquit qui non liberos suos incolumes et beatos esse cupiat. utique et folet fieri ut nemo sit qui non amet liberos suos: et attributum personae est. i. fortunae quae nominant. et ait: nemo est. Iu dicatu est res assensione: aut auctoritate: aut iudicio alicuius: aut aliquorum coprobata. Iam et hinc in tria diuisit iudicatu. Nam assensio in religione est: et approbatu. Religiosum est inquit: si quod de aliq iurati iu dices iudicarut: et io religiosum: quia iurati iudicarut: quod assentiri nos necesse est. Aiaduertamus tam ut iudiciu gestum semp negotio consequatur. Comune est quod omnes uulgus probarunt. Comune est i qt qd ex more uulgi iusti auctoritate tenet: ut necesse fit maioribus natu assurgat: ut suppliciu misere ri. Haec ut sequmur hemus uulgi auctoritate. Deid hoc et aiaduertaus et cosuetudo quae cuq rem semp consequatur. Inter id qd fere folet fieri: et comune hoc interest. Id quod fere folet fieri ex quada natura est. Comune iudicato stringit. Approbatu est quod hoies cu dubiu est: qle heri oportet.

# CHAPTER IV.

### The territory, towns, and castles of the Eugubini.

I. One would seek in vain what the boundaries of the Eugubine territory were in earlier times, when the Romans held power, and even more so before the Romans. This alone is clear: that whatever lay between these cities, the distance between which was not uniform—Sentinum, Tadinum, Nuceria, Assisium, Perusium, Tifernum, and Callium—pertained to the Eugubini. However, later, when the barbarians had disturbed the state of Italy, with Tadinum destroyed and other cities afflicted, the Eugubini gained this benefit from the common disaster: their reach extended beyond the ancient borders. Thus, a part of the Tadinum region seems to have been attributed to them, which I believe also happened with the Sentinum and Callium regions, and perhaps those of other cities. In no place, however, were the boundaries of the Eugubine territory extended more than on the side that lies between Callium and Sentinum, beyond Pergula, founded by them, and Mons Siccus, otherwise <term>Mons Siconis</term> <gloss>Mount Siconis</gloss>, which places lay beyond the borders of the Callium and Sentinum peoples and perhaps belonged to the Suafani, an ancient city situated on the bank of the river of the same name <margin>(a)</margin>, by which river the town of Per-

MY first care was to examine first the embouchure of wind Instruments, to understand well how one could draw sound from them, the parts that contributed to it, & how it could be modified.

You know, Gentlemen, that the embouchure of a Transverse Flute differs from that of other wind Instruments, such as the recorder, the flageolet, & the Organ Pipe, in that in the latter, the wind introduced into a narrow but determined hole strikes the particles of the Body of the Instrument that are found immediately below; namely, the Bizeau <note>original: "Bizeau" - the beveled edge or labium of an instrument</note>: & by the promptness of its return, & its reaction on the particles that surround it, it is forced to suffer a violent collision. Thus communicating its vibrations to all the particles of the wood of the Flute, which in their turn communicate them to all the surrounding exterior air, it produces in us the sensation of sound.

But the embouchure in the Transverse Flute is indeterminate, in that it consists in the emission of the wind through a more or less large opening formed by the moving apart or bringing together of the lips, their position more or less close to the hole of the Flute, or more or less advanced over the edge of this same hole.

That is to say, the highest degree of sympathetic vibration is only to be attained through introduced tones of very narrowly limited pitch. This is the case with tuning forks and bells. The air mass of the oral cavity, on the contrary, has low density and mass; its walls, as far as they are formed by soft tissues, are not very resistant and are imperfectly elastic, having much internal friction during vibrations, through which they destroy movement. Furthermore, the vibrated air mass of the oral cavity communicates through the mouth opening with the external air and quickly gives up large parts of its received movement to it. For this very reason, a once-excited vibrating movement in the air of the oral cavity dies out very quickly, as one can easily observe if one snaps a finger against the cheek with various vowel positions of the mouth. One then distinguishes the pitch of the resonance quite well for the various transition stages of <term>O</term> on one hand toward <term>U</term> and on the other toward <term>A</term>.
